hook: Every profile on this dating site borrows the words of real users, and not one of them belongs to a person.
lede: Online dating asks us to trust that the face and the words on the screen belong to someone. CARBON COPY puts that trust to the test. We built a fake dating platform whose profiles were all generated by AI, drawing on our study of how dating-app users present themselves, and invited visitors to browse, like and chat as if looking for a partner. The further they browsed, the less human the profiles became.

chapters.title: A dating site where no one is real
paragraphs: Generative AI can now produce convincing yet fictitious images, videos, texts and voices, and people often fail to recognize fake content such as AI-generated news or social media profiles. Fake accounts with AI-synthesized faces have already spread on platforms like Facebook and LinkedIn.

In mobile dating, the problem turns personal. Verifying who someone is becomes a matter of safety and trust, and it grows harder as the technology improves. CARBON COPY brings that problem into a setting visitors already know how to use: a dating app.

quote.text: What if the person you’re dating is a Generative AI profile?

chapters.title: Profiles written in borrowed words
paragraphs: The profiles were not invented from scratch. Drawing on our CSCW study of dating-app users, we analyzed how real users describe themselves and used ChatGPT to write profile text that mimics their language. That text then became the prompt for images of each AI persona in different scenarios.

To keep a character believable across a whole profile, the same face was swapped into all of their images, giving each persona a consistent identity from one situation to the next. The profiles were then arranged in a sequence, from highly realistic to progressively less human. A selection was also published on Instagram.

chapters.title: Like, skip, say hello
paragraphs: The website mirrors a familiar dating app, complete with options to like, skip and chat. Visitors rate the profiles, read their machine-generated text, and message them through a custom-prompted ChatGPT model, as if each one were a potential match.

The experience is designed as a slow turn. Visitors begin by trusting that the profiles belong to people. As their interactions deepen, subtle inconsistencies surface and unease grows, until they recognize that every profile is AI-created, fabricated in a way that feels “uncanny but familiar”. chapters.title: A room furnished from their photos
paragraphs: For the installation, a sketch map lays out a 240 × 280 cm room around the website: a bed, a floor lamp, a plant, two bean bags, a photo wall and a “Carbon Copy Dating” poster tiled with profile pictures. Visitors use the site on iPads, two on a central table and one on a side table.

The props scattered around the room, a stick, playing cards, a fishing rod and a guitar, are circled in the rendering and linked to profile photos that feature the same objects. The personas’ lives spill out of the screen and into the room.

figures.caption: Installation plan: a rendering of the room with its props highlighted, the 240 × 280 cm sketch map, the photo wall, and the profile poster.

chapters.title: What we reach for when we swipe
paragraphs: By watching how people treat these would-be partners, CARBON COPY probes how we use technology to fulfill emotional needs, turning the innate desire to connect into a technology-mediated interaction with the unreal. It asks visitors to reflect on the trust they place in digital personas, and on what follows as AI moves into uniquely human social ecosystems.
Seen beside our study of how people present themselves on dating apps, the work closes a loop: the way real users describe themselves becomes the raw material for partners who were never there.

quote.by: Project summary, Studio for Narrative Spaces

takeaways: In online dating, verifying who is on the other side is a matter of safety and trust, and it gets harder as generated profiles grow more convincing.
Built from the patterns of real users’ self-descriptions, fake personas can feel uncanny but familiar.
Experiencing the deception firsthand, rather than reading about it, invites reflection on the trust we place in digital personas.
